General Contractor Marketing: How to Win More Remodeling and Commercial Projects

Learn how to market your general contracting business. Includes portfolio marketing, commercial lead generation, architect relationships, and high-ticket project acquisition.

Most general contractors are invisible online until someone already knows their name. That is the core marketing problem — and it is costing you projects worth $50,000, $200,000, or more.

This guide covers the complete marketing system for general contractors who want to win high-ticket remodeling and commercial projects. You will learn how to build a portfolio that sells before you speak, how to generate commercial leads through LinkedIn and bidding platforms, how to turn architects into referral partners, and how to nurture prospects through a 3-to-12-month sales cycle without letting a single lead go cold.

Every strategy here is built for the reality of general contracting: long timelines, high stakes, relationship-driven decisions, and two completely different buyers — the homeowner remodeling their kitchen and the facilities director awarding a $400,000 commercial build-out.

Chapter 1: The General Contractor Buyer — Two Completely Different People

General contractors do not have one customer. They have two. And marketing to both with the same message is why most contractor websites convert at 2% when they should convert at 5-8%.

The Residential Remodeling Buyer

The homeowner considering a kitchen remodel, bathroom renovation, or whole-home renovation has a decision timeline of 3 to 9 months. According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR) Remodeling Report, 27% of homeowners remodel because surfaces and systems are worn out, 19% want energy efficiency improvements, and 18% are preparing to sell. The Houzz 2026 Home Renovation Report found that 79% of homeowners simply want to remain in their current home, and 62% expect to stay for 11+ years after renovating.

This buyer is emotionally invested. They are not just buying construction services — they are buying trust, peace of mind, and a finished space they will live in for years. Their research behavior is extensive: 70% compare prices online, 57% check availability, and 55% read reviews before contacting a contractor (Collective Measures 2026 Trends Report).

The median renovation spend in 2024 was $20,000, with the top 10% of remodelers spending $140,000+ per project (RubyHome, citing Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies data). Kitchen remodels median at $22,000, primary bathrooms at $13,000. The buyer who can afford these projects is typically Gen X (median spend: $25,000) or a Baby Boomer focused on aging-in-place modifications.

Key insight: 54% of homeowners cite high costs as their biggest barrier to starting a project, and 28% say finding trusted professionals is their primary concern (Houzz 2026). Your marketing must address cost transparency and trust-building before the first conversation.

The Commercial Project Buyer

The commercial buyer — a property manager, facilities director, developer, or business owner — operates on a completely different logic. Their timeline is 6 to 18 months. Their decision involves 6 to 13 stakeholders (SalesLeads Inc. research on B2B construction buying committees). Their primary concerns are budget adherence, schedule compliance, safety record, and liability protection.

The commercial buyer does not search "general contractor near me" at 10 PM. They search during business hours, evaluate proposals side-by-side, check references, and often require bonding and insurance verification before a conversation even begins. According to Loopio's 2026 RFP Statistics, the average RFP win rate across industries is 45%, but for cold commercial construction bids — where no pre-existing relationship exists — the win rate drops to 15% or less (TrebleHook analysis).

For incumbent contractors with established relationships, re-bid win rates climb to 60-90%. This is the critical insight: commercial construction marketing is not about winning more bids. It is about becoming the incumbent before the bid goes out.

The Architect/Designer as Influencer

There is a third player in both markets: the architect or interior designer. Homeowners frequently ask architects to recommend 2-3 general contractors they have worked with previously (Billdr.ai, citing industry practice). On commercial projects, architects influence contractor selection through design-build partnerships, construction manager recommendations, or direct referrals to the owner.

According to the AIA (American Institute of Architects), nearly 90% of architects agree that early collaboration between architect and contractor produces better project outcomes. Yet many contractors treat architects as obstacles rather than partners — a mistake that costs them referral opportunities worth hundreds of thousands of dollars annually.

Why Most Contractors Market to the Wrong Buyer

The typical contractor website speaks to no one in particular. It lists services ("We do kitchens, bathrooms, additions, and commercial work"), shows a handful of project photos, and includes a generic contact form. It does not speak to the homeowner's fear of budget overruns. It does not speak to the commercial buyer's need for schedule certainty. It does not speak to the architect's desire for collaborative problem-solving.

The result: low conversion rates, unqualified leads, and a pipeline dependent on word-of-mouth that cannot scale.

Chapter 2: Portfolio Marketing — Your Most Powerful (and Most Neglected) Sales Tool

Portfolio marketing is the single biggest differentiator between contractors who win high-ticket projects and those who compete on price. Yet most contractors treat their portfolio as an afterthought — a few photos dumped on a "Our Work" page with no story, no metrics, and no strategic purpose.

Why Portfolio Marketing Works

A general contractor's portfolio is not a photo gallery. It is proof of capability, process, and professionalism. For a homeowner spending $75,000 on a kitchen remodel, the portfolio answers the question: "Can you deliver what I want, on time, without destroying my house?" For a commercial buyer, it answers: "Have you done work at this scale, in this sector, with this complexity?"

The data supports this. Video content delivers 49% higher ROI than static images in construction marketing (Siana Marketing 2026 Construction Marketing ROI Report). Contractors who document projects with before/during/after photography and video testimonials close at significantly higher rates than those who do not. One industrial blasting contractor case study documented by Innovaxis showed that adding 6 case studies to their marketing mix contributed to $1.2 million in new customer revenue and a 735% marketing ROI over two years.

The Portfolio Marketing Framework

Here is a five-part framework for turning your project history into a lead-generation asset:

1. Document Every Project Systematically

Before work begins, capture the "before" state — not just one photo, but a full walkthrough video (2-3 minutes) showing the existing conditions. During construction, document key milestones: demolition, rough-in, framing, drywall, finishes. After completion, capture the finished space from multiple angles, ideally with the homeowner or business owner in the frame.

Tools that make this easier:

  • OpenSpace or StructionSite for 360-degree job site documentation
  • CompanyCam for photo organization and team sharing
  • A simple smartphone gimbal (DJI OM series, ~$100) for stabilized walkthrough videos

2. Structure Every Project as a Case Study

Every portfolio entry should follow a Problem-Solution-Result format:

  • The Challenge: What was the client's situation? ("A 1970s kitchen with failing plumbing, inadequate lighting, and no connection to the outdoor patio the homeowners wanted to use.")
  • The Solution: What did you do? ("Complete gut renovation including structural modification to open the kitchen to the patio, custom cabinetry, quartz countertops, and LED lighting design.")
  • The Result: What was the outcome with specifics? ("Completed in 8 weeks — 1 week ahead of schedule. Client reported using the outdoor patio 4x more often. Project came in 3% under budget due to value engineering on the backsplash material.")

3. Segment Your Portfolio by Buyer Type

Your website should have separate portfolio sections for residential remodeling and commercial projects. Within residential, segment by project type (kitchens, bathrooms, whole-home, additions, ADUs). Within commercial, segment by sector (office build-outs, retail, hospitality, industrial, healthcare).

This segmentation serves two purposes. First, it helps prospects find relevant examples quickly. Second, it signals specialization — a contractor with 12 kitchen remodels in their portfolio looks more credible for a kitchen project than a contractor with 2 kitchens, 3 bathrooms, 4 decks, and a commercial project.

4. Include Metrics and Social Proof

Every case study should include:

  • Project budget range (if the client permits)
  • Timeline (planned vs. actual)
  • Square footage
  • Specific materials or techniques used
  • A direct client quote or video testimonial
  • Any awards, certifications, or third-party recognition

5. Distribute Beyond Your Website

Your portfolio content should live in multiple places:

  • Google Business Profile: Upload before/after photo sets as posts
  • Instagram: Project reveal carousels and Reels
  • Houzz: Profile with full project documentation
  • LinkedIn: Commercial project case studies for B2B visibility
  • Proposals: PDF case studies attached to commercial bids
  • Email nurture sequences: Relevant case studies sent to prospects based on project type

Portfolio Website Structure

Your portfolio pages should follow this hierarchy:

Page Type Purpose Example
Portfolio Hub Overview of all work /portfolio
Category Pages Filtered by project type /portfolio/kitchen-remodels
Individual Project Pages Full case study with SEO /portfolio/downtown-loft-renovation
Video Gallery Testimonials and walkthroughs /portfolio/videos

Each individual project page should be optimized for local SEO with the city/neighborhood in the URL, title tag, and content. A page titled "Downtown Loft Renovation — Portland General Contractor" captures search intent for "loft renovation Portland" while building topical authority.

Real-World Example

Construction Marketing Experts (UK) documented a specialist building contractor who invested in heritage project portfolios, trade media coverage, and social media documentation. The result: a 38% direct mail response rate (30x the industry average) and £900,000 in new business attributed to portfolio-driven marketing.

Chapter 3: Local SEO for Contractors — Dominate the Map Pack Without a Storefront

Local SEO is the highest-ROI marketing channel for general contractors who serve a defined geographic area. The data is unambiguous: 46% of all Google searches are local (Changescape Web), and 64% of consumers use Google Business Profile for contact information (LocalLeads247).

For contractors, the Map Pack — the three local results that appear above organic listings — is prime real estate. A contractor ranking in Position 1 of the Map Pack receives significantly more calls and website clicks than one ranking in Position 4 or below.

Google Business Profile Optimization for Contractors

Claim and Verify

The first step is non-negotiable: claim and verify your Google Business Profile. According to LocalLeads247, 56% of local businesses have not claimed their free listing. If you have not claimed yours, you are already behind half your competitors.

Choose the Right Primary Category

Your primary category should be as specific as possible. "General Contractor" is acceptable, but if you specialize, use the more specific category:

  • "General Contractor" (broad)
  • "Remodeling Contractor" (residential focus)
  • "Commercial Contractor" (B2B focus)

Add 5-10 secondary categories that cover your service mix.

Service Area Configuration

General contractors are typically service-area businesses without a customer-facing storefront. Hide your physical address and define service areas by city or ZIP code. Do not overreach — listing a 100-mile radius when you only work within 30 miles damages your relevance signals and generates unqualified leads.

Photo Strategy

Businesses with photos receive 42% more direction requests and 35% more website clicks (Google Support data via The Contractor Elite). Your photo strategy should include:

  • Before/after project photos (uploaded as sets)
  • Team photos (builds trust)
  • Equipment and vehicle photos (signals professionalism)
  • Office/shop photos (if applicable)
  • Logo and cover image

Upload 5-10 new photos monthly. Geo-tag photos when possible.

Review Generation

Reviews are the #1 ranking factor for Map Pack position. Google weighs three factors:

  • Volume: Total number of reviews
  • Velocity: How quickly you are getting new reviews
  • Recency: 25 recent reviews beats 45 old reviews

Best practices for contractors:

  • Send SMS review requests 24-48 hours after project completion (not email — SMS has higher open rates)
  • Include a direct review link (use Google's review link generator)
  • Respond to every review within 48 hours
  • Never offer incentives for reviews — Google can detect and remove them

A fully completed and optimized Google Business Profile can increase leads by 40%, and consistent reviews add another 25% (Changescape Web).

Website Local SEO

NAP Consistency

Your Name, Address, and Phone number must be identical across your website, Google Business Profile, Yelp, BBB, Facebook, and every directory listing. Even small variations ("St." vs. "Street," "Suite 100" vs. "#100") confuse search engines and dilute ranking signals.

Location Pages

If you serve multiple cities, create dedicated location pages for each primary service area. Each page should include:

  • Unique content (not duplicated across pages)
  • City-specific project examples
  • Local landmarks or neighborhood references
  • City-specific service descriptions
  • Embedded Google Map
  • Local schema markup

Example: /services/kitchen-remodeling-portland and /services/kitchen-remodeling-beaverton — each with unique project photos, local testimonials, and neighborhood-specific content.

Local Business Schema

Implement LocalBusiness schema markup on your contact page and homepage. This structured data helps search engines understand your service area, business hours, services offered, and contact information — increasing your chances of appearing in rich results and AI Overviews.

Local Citations and Directories

Beyond Google, ensure consistent listings on:

  • Yelp for Business
  • Better Business Bureau (BBB)
  • HomeAdvisor / Angi (controversial but still relevant for visibility)
  • Houzz
  • Thumbtack
  • Local chamber of commerce directories
  • Industry-specific directories (NARI, NAHB)

Real-World Result

Double G Consulting documented a contractor who started at Position 11 in the Map Pack (effectively invisible). After a 6-step GBP optimization process, they reached Position 3 at 60 days and Position 1 at 90 days. Inbound calls from Google more than tripled with zero additional ad spend.

Chapter 4: Website Design That Converts High-Ticket Inquiries

A general contractor's website has one job: turn visitors into qualified leads. Not to win design awards. Not to showcase every project you've ever done. To generate inquiries from people who can afford your services and are ready to start a conversation.

The average contractor website converts at 2-4%. Top-performing contractor websites convert at 8-15% (PipelineOn 2026 benchmarks). For a remodeling contractor with a $50,000 average project value, the difference between 2% and 8% conversion on 500 monthly visitors is $120,000 in additional monthly revenue from the same traffic.

The High-Ticket Contractor Website Framework

Above the Fold: Immediate Clarity

The top section of your homepage must answer three questions in under 5 seconds:

  1. What do you do? ("Portland's Premier Residential Remodeling Contractor")
  2. Who do you serve? ("Kitchens, Bathrooms, and Whole-Home Renovations")
  3. What should I do next? ("Schedule a Free Consultation" or "Get an Estimate")

Your phone number must be visible and tap-to-call on mobile. 71% of contractor traffic is mobile (PipelineOn), and for emergency-adjacent searches, mobile share approaches 90%.

Portfolio Integration

Your best 3-6 projects should appear on the homepage, not buried on a separate page. Each project card should link to the full case study. This immediately answers the visitor's unspoken question: "Can they do work at my level?"

Service Pages with Depth

Each major service (kitchen remodeling, bathroom remodeling, commercial build-outs, etc.) deserves its own dedicated page of 800-1,500 words. These pages should include:

  • Process explanation (what happens week by week)
  • Typical timeline and budget range
  • Material and finish options
  • FAQ specific to that service
  • 2-3 relevant portfolio examples
  • Clear CTA (schedule consultation, request estimate)

Trust Signals

High-ticket buyers need proof before they inquire. Your website should display:

  • License numbers and state verification links
  • Insurance and bonding information
  • BBB accreditation
  • Industry certifications (NARI, NAHB, LEED)
  • Years in business
  • Number of projects completed
  • Client testimonials with full names and project details
  • "As seen in" media mentions

Quote Request System

Your contact form should be simple but strategic:

  • Name, phone, email (3 fields maximum for initial inquiry)
  • Project type dropdown
  • Budget range dropdown (qualifies leads without being intrusive)
  • Timeline dropdown
  • Project description (optional)

Follow up with a more detailed questionnaire after the initial inquiry, not before.

Financing Information

For projects over $25,000, financing is often the deciding factor. Display financing options prominently on service pages and include a financing calculator if possible. Contractors who display financing options see 12-20% higher contact rates on replacement and renovation pages (PipelineOn data).

Mobile Optimization

Mobile performance is not optional. Every 1-second delay in page load drops conversion by 7%, and 53% of mobile visitors abandon sites that take 3+ seconds to load (PipelineOn). Critical mobile requirements:

  • Sticky tap-to-call button (+25-40% call volume)
  • Mobile LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) under 2.5 seconds
  • Multi-step mobile forms (+30-60% completion vs. single-page forms)
  • Click-to-text option for younger homeowners

Speed and Technical Performance

Metric Target Why It Matters
Page load time Under 2.5 seconds Every second = -7% conversion
Mobile LCP Under 2.5 seconds ~2x conversion vs. 4.5s sites
Time to Interactive Under 3.8 seconds Prevents visitor abandonment
HTTPS Required Trust signal; ranking factor
Core Web Vitals All "Good" Google's page experience signal

Chapter 5: Commercial Lead Generation — LinkedIn, Bidding Platforms, and B2B Relationships

Commercial construction projects represent the highest-margin, most predictable revenue stream for general contractors who know how to market for them. The challenge is that commercial lead generation operates on a completely different model than residential marketing.

The Commercial Sales Cycle Reality

Commercial construction sales cycles range from 6 to 18 months. The buying committee includes 6 to 13 stakeholders: facilities directors, CFOs, project managers, procurement heads, safety directors, and sustainability officers (SalesLeads Inc. research). No single person makes the decision, and the contractor who builds relationships across the committee before the RFP is released has a massive advantage.

According to TrebleHook's analysis of construction RFP win rates, incumbent contractors with existing relationships win re-bids at 60-90% rates. Cold bids — where no pre-existing relationship exists — win at 15% or less. The implication is clear: commercial marketing is relationship marketing, not lead-generation marketing in the traditional sense.

LinkedIn for Commercial Contractors

LinkedIn is the most underutilized platform for general contractors pursuing commercial work. Only 0.2% of LinkedIn users publish articles, which means there is a massive content opportunity for contractors willing to share expertise.

Profile Optimization

Your personal LinkedIn profile should read like a commercial contractor's resume:

  • Headline: "Commercial General Contractor | $50M+ in Office, Retail, and Hospitality Build-Outs | Portland, OR"
  • About section: Project highlights, specialties, certifications, and a clear value proposition
  • Featured section: Case studies, project videos, media mentions
  • Experience: Quantified achievements ("Delivered 23 commercial projects on time and under budget")

Company Page

Post weekly updates featuring:

  • Project milestones and completions
  • Team highlights and safety achievements
  • Industry insights and commentary
  • Client testimonials (with permission)

LinkedIn Sales Navigator

For proactive commercial lead generation, LinkedIn Sales Navigator allows you to:

  • Identify facilities directors and property managers at target companies
  • Track job changes (a new facilities director is often a new opportunity)
  • Monitor company growth signals (hiring, expansion, new locations)
  • Build targeted prospect lists by geography, company size, and industry

LinkedIn Advertising

LinkedIn Lead Gen Forms simplify B2B lead capture with pre-filled forms, achieving 10-15% click-to-lead conversion rates. Cost per lead for commercial construction B2B typically runs $75-$250, which is justified when the average commercial project value is $100,000-$500,000+.

Target by job title (Facilities Director, Property Manager, VP of Construction, Development Manager), company size, and industry. Retarget website visitors who viewed your commercial services pages.

Commercial Bidding Platforms

Several platforms connect contractors with commercial project opportunities:

Platform Best For Cost
PlanHub Subcontractors bidding on GC projects Subscription-based
Dodge Construction Network Early project detection Premium subscription
Building Radar AI-driven project identification Subscription + usage
ConstructConnect Plan rooms and project leads Subscription
ISqFt Commercial plan distribution Subscription

The key to success on these platforms is not volume — it is selectivity. According to Loopio's 2026 RFP data, 71% of high-win teams use formal go/no-go qualification frameworks. Chasing every RFP dilutes win rates and burns proposal resources.

Property Manager Relationships

Property managers are the gatekeepers to recurring commercial work. A single property management company may oversee dozens of properties, each requiring ongoing maintenance, tenant improvements, and capital projects.

Building the Relationship

  1. Identify target property management firms in your service area using CoStar, LoopNet, or local commercial real estate databases
  2. Attend property management association events (IREM, BOMA local chapters)
  3. Offer preventive maintenance programs with scheduled inspections, priority response times, and discounted rates
  4. Provide documentation — work logs, photographic evidence, and detailed reporting that property managers need for their owners
  5. Propose a pilot project — a small job that demonstrates your reliability before larger commitments

Maintenance Contract Structure

Commercial maintenance contracts typically include:

  • Scope of work with specific, measurable tasks
  • Service Level Agreements (SLAs): 2-hour emergency response, 48-hour routine maintenance
  • Fixed monthly fees for predictable budgeting
  • 1-3 year terms with automatic renewal clauses
  • Insurance requirements: general liability ($1M-$3M), workers' compensation

Go/No-Go Qualification Framework

Before investing in any commercial proposal, score the opportunity on these criteria:

Criteria Weight Score (1-10)
Relationship strength 25%
Project fit with expertise 20%
Budget realism 15%
Timeline feasibility 15%
Competitive environment 15%
Strategic value (repeat potential) 10%

Minimum threshold: 70/100. Below this, decline politely and invest the saved time in relationship-building.

Chapter 6: Architect and Designer Relationships — The Referral Engine Most Contractors Ignore

Architects are the single most underutilized referral source for general contractors. Homeowners routinely ask architects to recommend 2-3 contractors. Commercial owners rely on architects to suggest qualified builders. Yet most contractors treat architects as adversaries — or ignore them entirely.

Why Architects Matter

According to the Architect Marketing Institute, 70-100% of an architect's future projects come from referrals. When an architect recommends a contractor, they are staking their professional reputation on that contractor's performance. This makes architect referrals highly qualified leads with pre-established trust.

The AIA reports that nearly 90% of architects believe early collaboration with contractors produces better outcomes. Contractors who position themselves as collaborative partners — not just executors of someone else's design — become the architects' first call.

What Architects Look for in Contractors

Architects evaluate contractors on specific criteria before recommending them:

Quality What It Means for Your Marketing
Experience and reputation Documented portfolio of similar projects, client references
Communication skills Responsiveness, clarity in emails and meetings, proactive updates
Technical knowledge Understanding of building codes, material properties, construction methods
Cost control Accurate estimating, change order transparency, budget adherence
Problem-solving Creative solutions to unexpected challenges, not just problems
Schedule adherence On-time delivery, realistic scheduling, buffer management
Safety record Low incident rates, proper training, insurance documentation

How to Build Architect Relationships

1. Start with Your Portfolio

Before reaching out to architects, ensure your portfolio showcases work that would impress a design professional. High-quality photography, attention to detail in finishes, and clean execution of complex design elements matter more to architects than to the average homeowner.

2. Attend AIA Events

Local AIA chapters host monthly events, continuing education sessions, and project tours. Attend consistently. Do not pitch — listen, ask questions, and demonstrate genuine interest in design. After 2-3 events, architects will recognize you, and conversations will flow naturally.

3. Offer Value First

Instead of asking for referrals, offer something useful:

  • "I noticed your firm specializes in historic renovations. We just completed a similar project with some interesting structural challenges. Would you be interested in seeing the photos?"
  • "I wrote a brief guide on cost-effective alternatives to specified materials that maintain design intent. Happy to share it with your team."
  • "We're hosting a lunch-and-learn on [topic] next month. Would your team be interested?"

4. Collaborate on Content

Propose co-authored content that benefits both parties:

  • "Architect vs. Contractor: How to Navigate Design Changes During Construction"
  • "5 Things Architects Wish Contractors Knew About Material Specifications"
  • "Case Study: How Early Contractor Involvement Saved $40K on a Kitchen Renovation"

This content can be published on both your websites, shared on LinkedIn, and used in email newsletters — doubling the exposure for the same effort.

5. Deliver Flawlessly on the First Project

The first project with a new architect is an audition. Every detail matters:

  • Show up to meetings prepared and on time
  • Flag potential issues early, not after they become problems
  • Respect the design intent — do not unilaterally substitute materials
  • Document everything with photos and written reports
  • Finish on time and on budget

One successful project with an architect can lead to 5-10 referrals over the next few years. One failed project can blacklist you from their network permanently.

Co-Marketing Opportunities

Once a relationship is established, explore formal co-marketing:

  • Joint portfolio pages on both websites
  • Shared project photography (with client permission)
  • Joint presentations at home shows or industry events
  • Referral agreements (formal or informal)
  • Social media cross-promotion

The Design-Build Advantage

Design-build project delivery — where the architect and contractor work as an integrated team under a single contract — is growing in popularity. According to Bowser Construction Group, design-build projects typically achieve 6-10% cost savings and faster completion times compared to traditional design-bid-build.

If you can offer design-build services or partner with an architect to do so, you differentiate yourself from contractors who only bid on completed plans. Market this capability prominently on your website and in commercial proposals.

Chapter 7: Content and Nurture Marketing — Staying Top-of-Mind for 3-12 Months

The general contractor's sales cycle is long. A homeowner who visits your website in January may not start their project until September. A commercial prospect who downloads your portfolio in Q1 may not release an RFP until Q4. If you are not nurturing these leads throughout the cycle, you are losing projects to competitors who stayed in touch.

Why Nurture Marketing Is Essential for Contractors

According to Venture Harbour's 2026 lead nurturing statistics, 48% of businesses say most of their leads require long-cycle nurturing. For construction specifically, sales cycles routinely stretch 6-12 months or longer (ZAG FIRST Marketing). Nurtured leads generate 50% more sales-ready opportunities at 33% lower cost than non-nurtured leads (Demand Gen Report).

The construction buyer's journey involves extensive research. 80% of Gen Z DIYers use YouTube for research, 61% of Gen X do the same, and 62% of Millennials do "a lot" or "a good amount" of research before hiring a contractor (Collective Measures 2026). Your content marketing job is to be present during that research phase — not just at the moment of decision.

Lead Scoring for Contractors

Not all leads are equal. Implement a simple lead scoring system:

Behavior Points
Visits pricing page +10
Downloads case study +15
Requests estimate +25
Opens 3+ emails in a week +10
Clicks CTA in email +15
Visits website 5+ times +20
Does not open emails for 30 days -10

Leads scoring 50+ points trigger a sales call. Leads scoring below 20 remain in nurture.

Blog SEO Strategy

Your blog should target keywords your prospects search during research:

  • "How much does [project] cost in [city]?"
  • "[Project] timeline and process"
  • "Best [material] for [application]"
  • "[City] building permit requirements"
  • "Contractor vs. handyman for [project]"

Each blog post should include:

  • 1,500+ words of substantive content
  • Original photography or diagrams
  • Local references and city-specific details
  • Internal links to relevant service pages
  • Clear CTA (schedule consultation, download guide)
  • FAQ schema markup for AI Overview optimization

Chapter 8: Paid Advertising — Google Ads, LinkedIn Ads, and Retargeting for Contractors

Paid advertising for general contractors requires channel-specific strategies. The same ad that works on Google Search will fail on LinkedIn, and vice versa. Understanding the intent behind each platform is the difference between profitable campaigns and wasted budget.

Google Ads for Contractors

Google Ads captures high-intent searches — people actively looking for a contractor right now. For general contractors, the most effective campaign types are:

Google Local Services Ads (LSAs)

LSAs appear at the very top of search results, above traditional paid ads and organic listings. They operate on a pay-per-lead model (not pay-per-click), and leads are typically $20-$50 for home services. Google verifies your license, insurance, and background check before you can run LSAs.

LSAs are particularly effective for remodeling contractors because:

  • They display your Google review rating prominently
  • You only pay for actual leads (phone calls or messages)
  • They appear for high-intent searches like "kitchen remodeler near me"
  • They include a "Google Guaranteed" badge that builds trust

Search Campaigns

Target keywords by intent level:

Intent Keywords Strategy
High "kitchen remodeling contractor [city]" Max bid, dedicated landing page
High "commercial general contractor [city]" Max bid, commercial landing page
Medium "how much does a kitchen remodel cost" Educational landing page + retargeting
Medium "best remodeling contractor [city]" Review-focused landing page
Low "kitchen design ideas" Blog content, not paid ads

Average cost per click for construction-related keywords is $6.45, with cost per lead averaging $89.30 (Siana Marketing 2026). For a contractor with a $50,000 average project and 40% close rate, a $90 lead that converts to a $20,000 gross margin project is extraordinarily profitable.

Smart Bidding Strategies

For 2026, Google's Smart Bidding requires 30+ conversions per month for optimal performance. If you are below this threshold, start with Maximize Conversions and transition to Target CPA once you have sufficient data.

Strategy Best For Requirement
Maximize Conversions New campaigns, lead generation No minimum
Target CPA Established campaigns 30+ conversions/month
Maximize Conversion Value High-ticket, variable pricing Conversion value tracking

Retargeting

95% of website visitors do not convert on their first visit (industry average). Retargeting brings them back through:

  • Display ads on websites they visit after leaving yours
  • YouTube ads showing your best project videos
  • Discovery ads in Gmail and Google Discover

Budget allocation recommendation: 60% to cold audience acquisition, 40% to retargeting.

LinkedIn Ads for Commercial Contractors

LinkedIn is the only platform where you can reliably reach facilities directors, property managers, and development executives. For commercial general contractors, LinkedIn ads should focus on:

Sponsored Content

  • Case studies of completed commercial projects
  • Whitepapers on commercial construction trends
  • "How we solved [specific problem]" content

Lead Gen Forms

  • Pre-filled forms reduce friction
  • 10-15% click-to-lead conversion rates
  • Best for gated content: "2026 Commercial Build-Out Cost Guide"

Message Ads (InMail)

  • Personalized messages to targeted prospects
  • Use sparingly — overuse damages brand perception
  • Best for event invitations or high-value content offers

LinkedIn cost per lead ($75-$250) is higher than Google, but the average commercial project value ($100,000-$500,000+) justifies the investment.

Social Media Advertising

Facebook/Instagram

Best for residential remodeling awareness and visual project displays:

  • Carousel ads showing before/after transformations
  • Video ads of project walkthroughs
  • Lead ads for estimate requests
  • Geo-targeting to specific neighborhoods or income levels

YouTube

YouTube ads deliver 25% higher video views and 20% better engagement than other platforms for home services (Collective Measures 2026). Effective YouTube ad formats:

  • 6-second bumper ads with brand awareness
  • 15-30 second skippable ads showing project highlights
  • Longer-form content for retargeting audiences

Budget Recommendations by Company Size

Company Size Monthly Ad Budget Primary Channels
Solo contractor / small crew $500-$1,500 Google LSAs, GBP
5-15 employees $2,000-$5,000 Google Search + LSAs, retargeting
15-50 employees $5,000-$12,000 Google, Facebook, limited LinkedIn
50+ employees / commercial focus $10,000-$30,000 Google, LinkedIn, YouTube, retargeting

Chapter 9: Tracking and Optimization — Measuring What Actually Matters

Marketing without measurement is guessing. General contractors who track the right metrics make better decisions, allocate budget more effectively, and scale what works while cutting what does not.

The Contractor Marketing Metrics Dashboard

Track these metrics monthly:

Metric How to Calculate Target
Website conversion rate Leads / Website visitors 5-8% (residential), 3-5% (commercial)
Cost per lead (CPL) Marketing spend / Total leads <$100 (residential), <$250 (commercial)
Cost per project acquired Marketing spend / Projects won <$1,250
Lead-to-consultation rate Consultations / Leads 60-80%
Consultation-to-proposal rate Proposals sent / Consultations 70-90%
Proposal win rate Projects won / Proposals sent 30-50% (residential), 15-40% (commercial)
Average project value Total revenue / Projects Track by source
Marketing ROI (Revenue from marketing - Marketing cost) / Marketing cost 400%+
Lead response time Time from inquiry to first contact <5 minutes

Lead Source Attribution

Know where your best projects come from:

Source Tracking Method
Google Business Profile UTM parameters + call tracking number
Google Ads Conversion tracking + offline conversion import
Organic search Google Search Console + UTM parameters
Referrals CRM source field + "How did you hear about us?"
Architect referrals Dedicated CRM tag + relationship tracking
LinkedIn UTM parameters + lead form tracking
Direct mail Unique phone number or landing page

Call Tracking

Use dynamic number insertion (DNI) to display different phone numbers based on traffic source. This allows you to attribute calls to specific marketing channels. Tools like CallRail, CallTrackingMetrics, or Invoca integrate with Google Ads and CRMs for closed-loop attribution.

CRM for Contractors

A CRM is essential for managing long sales cycles. Recommended options:

CRM Best For Cost
JobNimbus Contractors, project management integration $39-$99/user/month
Buildertrend Custom home builders, remodelers $99-$399/month
CoConstruct High-end residential $99-$299/month
HubSpot Commercial/B2B focus Free-$800+/month
Salesforce Enterprise commercial $75-$300/user/month

Your CRM should track:

  • Lead source
  • Project type and budget
  • Decision timeline
  • All touchpoints (calls, emails, meetings)
  • Proposal status
  • Win/loss reason

Speed-to-Lead

Response time is the most underappreciated metric in contractor marketing. 78% of homeowners hire the first company that responds to them. Responding within 60 seconds increases conversion by 391%. Waiting 5+ minutes kills 80% of qualifying odds (PipelineOn 2026).

Speed-to-Lead System:

  1. Auto-responder email within 60 seconds of form submission
  2. Text message alert to sales team immediately
  3. Phone call within 5 minutes during business hours
  4. After-hours: automated text response with next-day appointment scheduling

Monthly Optimization Routine

Week 1 of each month:

  1. Review last month's metrics dashboard
  2. Identify top 3 lead sources by volume and by project value
  3. Identify bottom 3 sources — reduce or eliminate spend
  4. Review website conversion rates by landing page
  5. Update ad creative if CTR drops below 2%
  6. Add new portfolio projects and case studies
  7. Review and respond to all reviews from previous month

Quarterly:

  1. Audit Google Business Profile for accuracy
  2. Refresh location page content
  3. Review and update email nurture sequences
  4. Analyze proposal win/loss data for patterns
  5. Survey 3-5 recent clients for feedback on marketing touchpoints

Conclusion: Your 90-Day Action Plan

General contractor marketing is not about doing everything at once. It is about building a system that compounds over time. Here is your 90-day roadmap:

Days 1-30: Foundation

  • [ ] Claim and fully optimize Google Business Profile
  • [ ] Audit website for mobile performance and conversion elements
  • [ ] Implement call tracking and CRM lead source tracking
  • [ ] Document 3-5 recent projects as full case studies
  • [ ] Set up automated email response within 60 seconds

Days 31-60: Visibility

  • [ ] Launch Google Local Services Ads
  • [ ] Begin weekly Google Business Profile posts with project photos
  • [ ] Implement review generation system (SMS-based)
  • [ ] Create service-specific landing pages for top 3 services
  • [ ] Attend first AIA or industry networking event

Days 61-90: Scale

  • [ ] Launch Google Search campaigns for high-intent keywords
  • [ ] Set up retargeting pixels and campaigns
  • [ ] Build email nurture sequence for new leads
  • [ ] Connect with 20 architects on LinkedIn with personalized messages
  • [ ] Establish monthly metrics review routine

Key Takeaways

  1. Market to your buyer, not to everyone. Residential and commercial prospects need completely different messaging, channels, and nurturing.
  2. Your portfolio is your best salesperson. Document every project as a case study with Problem-Solution-Result format, metrics, and testimonials.
  3. Relationships beat cold bids. Commercial construction win rates for incumbents are 60-90% vs. 15% for cold bids. Invest in relationship-building before the RFP.
  4. Architects are referral machines. One strong architect relationship can generate 5-10 qualified referrals per year. Treat the first project as an audition.
  5. Speed wins. The first contractor to respond gets the job 78% of the time. Build systems, not habits, for lead response.
  6. Measure everything. Marketing ROI of 400%+ is achievable when you track sources, optimize conversion rates, and double down on what works.

The contractors who win in 2026 are not the ones with the biggest budgets. They are the ones with the most systematic approach to attracting, nurturing, and converting high-ticket prospects. Start with the foundation. Build the system. Let it compound.
